extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent prosecutors, litigators, USPTO staff, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains the statutory and procedural standards governing post-issuance patent review under the Leahy‑Smith America Invents Act (inter partes review, post‑grant review, and reexamination), including institution thresholds, estoppel, burdens, timing, discovery, and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of patent owner written statements in reexamination (§301)
rubrics_metrics.description: Written statements of the patent owner filed in a proceeding before a Federal court or the USPTO regarding claim scope may be cited in a reexamination proceeding to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such written statements and related materials “shall not be considered by the Office for any purpose other than to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim.” The Committee explained these additions are intended to counteract patent owners offering differing interpretations of prior art in different proceedings, and specifically not to serve as a basis for institution of a reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-art basis for instituting reexamination (patents or printed publications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reexamination proceedings continue to be available only on the basis of “patents or printed publications.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Committee footnote states the scope of “patent and printed publication” prior art in amended §301 is intended to be coextensive with these terms in current §102; other AIA amendments are not intended to change that particular prior‑art basis for initiating reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director-initiated reexamination (§303) source expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may use patents-and-printed-publications prior art identified under additional statutory citations (including §302) to identify a substantial new question of patentability and order a reexamination on his own initiative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the AIA adds a citation to §302, the text observes it may have no substantive effect because §302 itself limits the basis to prior art cited under §301. The Director must determine whether a substantial new question of patentability is raised to order reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes review institution threshold: reasonable likelihood of success
rubrics_metrics.description: The threshold for instituting an inter partes review is elevated to require petitioners to present information showing their challenge has a “reasonable likelihood of success.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This replaces the prior “significant new question of patentability” standard. Satisfaction of the new threshold is assessed based on information presented in both the petition and the patent owner’s response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel in inter partes review: 'reasonably could have raised'
rubrics_metrics.description: A party that uses inter partes review is estopped from raising in a subsequent PTO proceeding any issue that it raised or reasonably could have raised in the inter partes review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This estoppel (often called ‘could-have-raised’ estoppel) applies to subsequent PTO proceedings such as ex parte reexamination or later inter partes review and was intended as a disincentive to serial challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of pre‑1999 limitations for IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA repealed the 1999 limit so that all patents (not only those with effective filing dates on/after Nov. 29, 1999) can be challenged in inter partes review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inter partes review takes effect on the statutory effective date specified by the AIA and pre‑AIA chapter 31 continues to govern requests filed before that date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in inter partes review: preponderance of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: In inter partes review, petitioners bear the burden of proving a patent is invalid by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee summarized this as a statutory change distinguishing administrative PTO review from the higher burdens sometimes applicable in district-court litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing constraints for invoking IPR during litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties seeking to use inter partes review during litigation must petition within 12 months of being served with a complaint alleging infringement; filing a declaratory judgment action bars seeking or maintaining an IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petitioner who files a declaratory judgment action is barred from seeking or maintaining IPR, and any DJ action will be stayed until the patent owner countersues for infringement. These rules are intended to coordinate IPR with district-court litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery rules in inter partes review
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may depose witnesses submitting affidavits or declarations and seek such other discovery as the Patent Office determines is otherwise necessary in the interest of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee emphasized limited but available discovery (including depositions) subject to PTAB control and the interest‑of‑justice standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-to-decision limits for inter partes review (12–18 months)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter partes review must be completed within 1 year of institution, but the Office may extend the deadline by 6 months for good cause (effectively a 12 to 18 month time frame).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory deadlines are intended to expedite resolution of post‑grant administrative proceedings; extensions are possible for good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to oral hearing in inter partes review
rubrics_metrics.description: Each party has the right to request an oral hearing as part of an inter partes review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral hearings are part of the adjudicative character of IPRs and provide parties an opportunity to present argument before the panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three‑judge PTAB (APJ) panels and appeal route
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter partes reviews are conducted before a panel of three administrative patent judges (APJs), and decisions are appealed directly to the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural design treats IPR as an adjudicative PTO proceeding with streamlined appellate review to the Federal Circuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant review scope and timing (first 12 months)
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA creates post‑grant review available during the first 12 months after grant (or issue of a reissue patent) allowing a challenge on any ground related to invalidity under 35 U.S.C. §282.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post‑grant review is intended to enable early challenges to patents on any §282 ground while protecting inventors from open‑ended, lifetime administrative attacks; the Committee note contains some discrepancies about the precise month count in earlier drafts (9 vs 12 months).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant review estoppel (raised and could have raised)
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner who completes a post‑grant review will be estopped in civil action from raising not only issues that were raised and decided in the review, but also those issues that the petitioner could have raised in the post‑grant review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This estoppel is broader than some prior estoppel standards and was highlighted as a significant consequence of completing a post‑grant review.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO rulemaking discretion and required considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many elements of the new proceedings are to be implemented through regulations, and the USPTO has substantial discretion in construing and applying statutory text of chapters 31 and 32.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AIA lists considerations the Office must weigh when promulgating regulations (codified at 35 U.S.C. §§316(b), 326(b)), which gives the Office latitude in procedural and implementation choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on number of instituted reviews in first four years
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA allows the USPTO to set a limit on the number of inter partes and post‑grant reviews that are instituted during the first four years after the proceedings take effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 6(c)(2)(B) and 6(f)(2)(B) authorize this limit; the text notes in the case of inter partes review the limit cannot be lower than a statutory floor (the document observes a specific floor but the sentence is truncated in this excerpt). The provision was intended to manage Office workload during initial implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No involuntary conversion from inter partes requests to ex parte reexamination (legislative history nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier bill versions would have allowed the Director to initiate ex parte reexamination based on art submitted in a request for inter partes reexamination (potentially converting third‑party requests into ex parte proceedings); that citation was eliminated in the final AIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The change likely reflects objections to involuntary conversion of inter partes requests into ex parte reexaminations and indicates legislative sensitivity about which submissions can trigger Director‑initiated ex parte proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals from ex parte reexamination and removal of §145 cross‑reference (§306)
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA amended §306 by striking §145 as one of the provisions under which a patentee may seek court review of an adverse PTAB decision on review of an ex parte reexamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The deletion eliminated a potential ambiguity about a patentee’s right to de novo district court review under §145 from adverse BPAI/PTAB decisions on ex parte reexamination; the legislative history explains this was intended to conform prior amendments that restricted review routes.
